clue.text: Spacemen's objective will show if it is !

definitions.text: Spacemen's objective will show if it is !

parts.words: Spacemen's objective will show if it is
parts.note: astronauts aim a launch at our satellite, and the second half also reads as that satellite being hot, so 'it will show if it is' teases the split 4-4

explanation.surface: A remark that a space mission's goal will become plain only if it really exists.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as MOONS HOT the entry hints that the moon will show itself if it is hot (glowing); read whole it is a launch aimed at the moon, the spacemen's objective.
explanation.definitionFit: A launch aimed at reaching the moon is exactly the target of astronauts, a lunar mission.

parts.note: Sir Thomas More, Henry VIII's Lord Chancellor and author of Utopia
something over is finished or ended

explanation.surface: Apart from anything else, the famous knight's career has come to an end.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Thomas More was executed by Henry VIII in 1535, which suits 'is finished'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words add a further point to an argument: in addition, furthermore.

parts.note: people who begin learning late in life, students of advanced age

explanation.definitionFit: The word, from Greek for late and learning, names those who take up study only in old age.

parts.note: a line of Thomas Gray's Ode on the Death of a Favourite Cat with a name missing: neither the tomcat nor the maid heard the drowning cat

explanation.definitionFit: In Gray's ode the servant who failed to hear the drowning cat is a maid with this name.

clue.text: Love in repose can be so laborious !

parts.note: love is nil in tennis, shaped like the letter O

indicators.note: the letters of the word repose are said to be capable of becoming something else, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Even lovemaking in a state of rest can be hard work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Love' is O, zero in tennis; 'can be' says the letters of 'repose' may become another word, and they make PEROSE to follow it.
explanation.definitionFit: The rare adjective describes work that is tedious and toilsome, requiring great effort.

definitions.note: the phrase completes the idiom with the clue's final word: the one left over or excluded is the one you throw out

parts.note: rum in the old British sense means strange or peculiar
a chap is a man

explanation.surface: Someone finds a strange fellow and wants him thrown out of the room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rum' looks like the drink, but in British English it means strange. The entry is completed by the idiom 'odd man out', the one excluded, which 'chuck him out' points to.
explanation.definitionFit: The odd one in a group is the person left over, the one excluded or thrown out.

clue.text: Not that this leader is mob-capped !

definitions.text: Not that this leader is mob-capped !

parts.words: Not that this leader is mob-capped
parts.note: a mob-cap is an old woman's bonnet; this leader is not wearing one but heads the mob

explanation.walkthrough: A mob-cap is a frilled cotton bonnet once worn indoors by women. The leader is not capped with one; he caps (heads) the mob.
explanation.definitionFit: A rabble-rousing leader who sways a crowd is literally a leader of the mob.

indicators.note: aimed wildly means the letters fly off in a disordered pattern

explanation.surface: Reporters are accused of shooting their stories at random.
explanation.definitionFit: Press, radio and television are the means that communicate news to the public.

clue.text: When it's up, you've had it !

definitions.text: When it's up, you've had it !

parts.words: When it's up, you've had it
parts.note: the idiom 'your ... is up' means your time has come and you are done for

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'your time is up' uses this word for the figure fate has assigned you.

parts.note: the island's French-coast name, split after its first letter, reads as a flat refusal to let you in, so it is ground you may not enter

explanation.walkthrough: The island is Ouessant, off the tip of Brittany at the mouth of the English Channel; split after its first letter its English name reads as 'you shall not', a ban.
explanation.definitionFit: The island off the tip of Brittany has a name that reads as the prohibition 'you shall not'.

definitions.note: read as 'opposition is', with the noun standing for the people who oppose

parts.note: re is the Latin-derived word meaning concerning or about
in British hospitals senior nurses are called sisters

explanation.surface: Political opponents are worried about how hospital nurses are treated.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is', a link. 'Nursing staff' gives SISTERS: in Britain a sister is a senior nurse in charge of a ward.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who resist form the opposition, people standing against something.

clue.text: Call me back, I'll still be the same !

definitions.note: a word used to address a woman politely, as in the musical title 'Call Me ...'

indicators.text: back, I'll still be the same
indicators.note: the clue says the word, read from its far end, stays unchanged, which marks a word identical in both directions

parts.note: a word used to address a woman politely, as in the musical title 'Call Me ...'

explanation.surface: Someone says that whichever way you address them they will not change.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a polite form of address ('call me ...'); the rest says the word reads the same from either end.
explanation.definitionFit: A courteous form of address for a woman is what she might ask to be called.

clue.text: Big fellow with the makings of a stoneworker

indicators.note: the makings are the raw material, so the letters of the stoneworker's title are rearranged into something new

parts.note: a mason is a worker in stone

explanation.surface: A large man looks like he could become a builder in stone.
explanation.walkthrough: Rearrange MASON, the stoneworker, to get the name. Osman I founded the Ottoman dynasty, and the name was borne by great Turkish rulers and generals: a 'big fellow' in history.
explanation.definitionFit: Osman I, founder of the Ottoman empire, was a great figure of history, a man of stature.

clue.text: Drink from a grandee with love

parts.note: love is nil in tennis scoring, shaped like the letter O

indicators.note: the drink is made from these letters, so they are reworked into it

explanation.surface: A Spanish nobleman offers a drink with affection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From' signals the anagram: A GRANDEE rearranged gives RANGEADE, and O ('love', zero in tennis) goes in front.
explanation.definitionFit: A fizzy orange-flavoured soft drink is a beverage.

parts.note: the House of Lords is called 'upstairs' to the Commons; giving someone a peerage, a rank by name, sends them there

explanation.walkthrough: In British politics the House of Lords is the upper house, so being given a title moves a politician 'upstairs'.
explanation.definitionFit: To grant a noble rank to someone is to raise them to the peerage, sending them up to the Lords.

clue.text: Spain's the place for these old stagers

indicators.note: the letters are to be placed afresh, giving room for the actors

parts.note: the possessive here keeps its S as a letter of the fodder

explanation.surface: Retired actors are told that Spain is the country to settle in.
explanation.walkthrough: SPAIN'S THE, placed differently, spells the actors. 'Old stagers' are veterans, here literally people of the stage.
explanation.definitionFit: Actors are people of the stage, so veteran actors are old stagers in a literal sense.

parts.note: big cats that growl, whose striped coats are all alike, as if in uniform

explanation.walkthrough: 'Uniform' suggests soldiers or police; here it is the stripes every one of these big cats wears.
explanation.definitionFit: The big striped cats growl and wear coats so alike they are a natural uniform.

parts.note: wilful obstruction is usually an offence against the police; here the police block the highway deliberately

explanation.walkthrough: 'Wilful obstruction' is a legal phrase for hindering the police; here the police themselves do the obstructing.
explanation.definitionFit: A barrier police set across a highway to stop traffic is a deliberate blockage.

clue.text: Been round about the grip? Much obliged

indicators.note: the first word goes round the outside of the grip, enclosing it

parts.note: taken as written
a grip is a hold

explanation.surface: Someone has wrapped up a handshake and is very grateful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round about' wraps the first word around the grip; 'about the' also reads as a mere link, but together with 'round' it is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling indebted to someone for a favour is being obligated to them.

parts.note: willow shoots are woven into baskets, so the plants make them

explanation.walkthrough: The makers are not weavers but the willow plants whose rods are woven.
explanation.definitionFit: Willows grown for their pliant shoots supply the material that baskets are woven from.

clue.text: Haggard heroine enfolds an Irishman in green

definitions.note: noun here: a piece of plant greenery

indicators.note: the heroine wraps round the Irishman, holding him inside

parts.note: She is the title heroine of H. Rider Haggard's novel
Pat is the stock name for an Irishman

explanation.surface: A novel's heroine embraces an Irishman wearing green.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Haggard' looks like gaunt, but it is the novelist H. Rider Haggard, whose 'She' supplies the outside letters round PAT.
explanation.definitionFit: The large leaflike bract sheathing a flower such as an arum is often a piece of greenery.

clue.text: Umpire in polite disagreement with the introduction

indicators.note: the umpire is set inside the expression of disagreement

parts.note: pace, from Latin, means 'with due respect to', used when politely disagreeing with someone
ref, short for referee, is a match official like an umpire

explanation.surface: A match official argues courteously with the opening remarks.
explanation.walkthrough: Pace (said PAH-chay), Latin for 'with peace', is put before a name when politely contradicting someone; 'in' sets the referee inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The opening section of a book is its foreword, the introduction.

clue.text: Hasn't much colour, the resident doctor in island capital

parts.note: something paler has less colour
MO is Medical Officer, the doctor attached to a unit

explanation.surface: A doctor living in an island's chief city looks rather pale.
explanation.walkthrough: MO, Medical Officer, is the doctor resident in a regiment or institution.
explanation.definitionFit: The chief city of Sicily, an island, is its capital.

clue.text: Has not a change become necessary for Lucy?

indicators.note: the letters of the first two words undergo a change of order

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether it is time to make changes for a woman named Lucy.
explanation.walkthrough: Lucy Ashton is the heroine of Scott's The Bride of Lammermoor, so her surname is what the name Lucy needs.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucy Ashton is the heroine of Walter Scott's novel, so that surname completes her name.

parts.note: a very small pearl is a minor jewel, and pearls cast before swine go unappreciated, so a young pig would not value one

explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'pearls before swine' says pigs cannot value fine things; a piglet, a young pig, gets the smallest pearl.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiny pearl used in jewellery is a small ornament, wasted on swine in the proverb.

indicators.note: a part taken out of the word, a sample of it, gives the creature

explanation.surface: Someone asks for a specimen of an Icelandic animal.
explanation.walkthrough: There are no such animals in Iceland: the large African antelope is just a sample of the word Icelandic.
explanation.definitionFit: An African antelope is one of the animals, a member of the fauna.

parts.note: Launcelot is the clown, Shylock's servant, in The Merchant of Venice

explanation.definitionFit: Launcelot's surname in The Merchant of Venice is this, the comic servant of Shylock.

definitions.meaning: a grip is an old word for a travelling bag

explanation.definitionFit: To clutch is to seize, and a grip is also a holdall or travel bag, so bags are luggage.

parts.note: a rugby player is awarded a cap for playing for their country; a jewelled head ornament is a cap of a grander kind

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rugby cap' suggests the cap a player wins for his country; the question mark says the cap is a head ornament set with jewels.
explanation.definitionFit: A jewelled crown worn by a woman on formal occasions is a decorated head ornament.

clue.text: Audacity displayed in a Balaclava helmet perhaps ?

definitions.text: Audacity displayed in a Balaclava helmet perhaps ?

parts.words: Audacity displayed in a Balaclava helmet perhaps
parts.note: a woollen helmet worn against the cold is a tough hood, and split that way the word for daring appears

explanation.walkthrough: A Balaclava helmet is a knitted hood covering head and neck; split 5-4 the answer reads as a 'hardy hood'. Balaclava is also the Crimean battle of the Charge of the Light Brigade, famous for daring.
explanation.definitionFit: Boldness or daring is shown by the brave, and audacity is a synonym for that quality.

parts.note: someone who wears no clothes has only dust on his body for a covering

explanation.walkthrough: The letters of IN DUST also rearrange to the answer, but nothing in the clue signals an anagram, so the whole clue is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: One who goes unclothed by choice has nothing on him but whatever settles there, like dust.

parts.note: a line from Milton's Lycidas with one word missing, to be supplied from the poem

explanation.definitionFit: Milton's Lycidas writes of the early primrose that dies abandoned, and the missing word means abandoned.
